newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal pilots threaten further strikes.
newsitem.headline: Portugal pilots threaten further strikes.

text.p: Striking pilots at state carrier TAP-Air Portugal grounded international flights for a second day on Friday and threatened to call further stoppages if the loss-making airline did not meet their demands.

A company spokesman said that by mid-morning TAP had cancelled six international flights from Lisbon, creating havoc as passengers tried to leave the country on Portugal's Revolution Day national holiday.
The 48-hour strike stranded 5,000 passengers from 39 cancelled flights on Thursday.

The president of the Union of Civil Aviation Pilots (SPAC) Joao Soeiro told the daily Publico the union would call a meeting to decide on further strike action if no solution for the dispute over working hours had been reached by the end of the day.
Soeiro, whose union represents the company's 430 pilots, said participation in the strike had been "excellent".
A last-ditch bid to break the deadlock failed on Wednesday night and TAP has called on the government to intervene in the dispute.

The strike has mainly affected international flights. Private carrier Portugalia handles most domestic flights, while the law obliges TAP pilots to maintain a limited service between the mainland and Portugal's Atlantic Azores and Madeira islands.

TAP, which says the strike is illegal, was offering no refunds for grounded flights. On Thursday stranded French tourists hired cars to make the 25-hour drive from the northern city of Oporto back to Paris.
The airline, which the Socialist government wants to privatise next year, is seeking greater flexibility in working hours in an attempt to boost efficiency and cut costs.
Pilots say they already work more than colleagues with rival European airlines and increasing their workloads threatened the safety of planes.

TAP lost 10.5 billion escudos ($61 million) in 1996. It had been hoping to make a profit for the first time in 23 years in 1997 in preparation for the proposed privatisation, but the company says the two-day stoppage will cost some $6.0 million and wipe out all the expected gain.

The company, one of the few European airlines not to form part of an international alliance, has been holding talks with various potential partners. But it says there is no chance of a deal until the issue of working hours is resolved.
The strike also poses the first serious labour challenge to the Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres since it took power 18 months ago.
